content: Potassium sorbate is the potassium salt derived from sorbic acid, primarily utilized as a food preservative and identified by the E number 202. It is widely effective in various applications, including food preservation, winemaking, and personal care products. The molecular formula of potassium sorbate is C6H7O2K, and its systematic chemical name is potassium (E,E)-hexa-2,4-dienoate. It has a molecular weight of 150.22 g/mol and exhibits high solubility in water, with a solubility rate of 58.2% at 20°C. Potassium sorbate is synthesized through the chemical reaction of sorbic acid with potassium hydroxide. In terms of its applications, potassium sorbate is extensively used to inhibit the growth of molds and yeasts in a variety of food products, including cheese, wine, yogurt, dried meats, baked goods, and dried fruits. It is also commonly found in herbal dietary supplements, where it prevents microbial growth and extends shelf life without posing any known health risks at typical usage levels. On ingredient labels, it is listed as potassium sorbate. Additionally, it is frequently incorporated into personal care products to prevent microbial contamination and enhance shelf stability. Some manufacturers have adopted potassium sorbate as an alternative to parabens in these products. In winemaking, potassium sorbate is often referred to as a wine stabilizer. When added to wine, it produces sorbic acid, which serves two critical purposes. First, after the active fermentation process has concluded and the wine has been clarified, potassium sorbate prevents any remaining yeast from reproducing. While existing yeast cells may continue fermenting residual sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, no new yeast cells will form once the current population dies. Second, when sweetening wine prior to bottling, potassium sorbate is used in conjunction with potassium metabisulfite to prevent refermentation. This is particularly important for sweet wines, sparkling wines, and certain hard ciders, though it may also be used in table wines that struggle to maintain clarity after fining. However, it is worth noting that some molds, such as certain strains of Trichoderma and Penicillium, as well as some yeasts, can detoxify sorbates through decarboxylation, leading to the production of 1,3-pentadiene. This compound can impart an undesirable keroseneor petroleum-like odor. From a toxicological perspective, potassium sorbate is regarded as safe due to its long-standing safety record and non-toxic nature. It is non-irritating and non-sensitizing, with allergic reactions being rare. It is also well-tolerated when consumed internally.
